concepts.name: Testing Pydantic AI agents with `TestModel` and `override`
Confused deputy attacks on MCP proxy servers

questions.prompt: An agent's action is typed `Annotated[Search | Reply | Handoff, Field(discriminator="kind")]`, and each model has a `kind: Literal[...]` field. The model returns `{"kind": "reply"}` without `Reply`'s required `text` field. What does Pydantic v2 do?

choices.text: Tries all three models left to right and reports errors from each one
Raises `union_tag_invalid`, because the payload fails its matching model
Validates only against `Reply` and reports that model's errors alone
Picks whichever model has the most valid fields, as smart mode does

questions.explanation: With a discriminator, Pydantic reads `kind` and tries only the matching member, so the error is just `Reply`'s missing `text`. Trying every member left to right and picking the best match is smart mode, the default for a plain union. `union_tag_invalid` is for a tag that matches no member, not for a member that fails.

sources.title: Unions
sources.claim: With a discriminated union only one member is tried, based on the discriminator, and validation errors are produced only for the matching case; plain unions default to smart mode, which tries members to find the best match.

questions.prompt: Your app calls a module-level Pydantic AI `support_agent` deep inside `handle_ticket()`. A unit test must run it with no real model call, and fail loudly if anything still tries to make one. What do you do?

choices.text: Set `models.ALLOW_MODEL_REQUESTS = False` alone, which swaps in a test model
Wrap the call in `support_agent.override(model=TestModel())` and block requests
Add a `model` parameter to `handle_ticket()` so the test can pass in `TestModel()`
Unset the provider API key in the test, so any real request fails at once

questions.explanation: `Agent.override` replaces an agent's model (or dependencies or toolsets) inside your application code without changing the agent's definition or your function signatures, and `TestModel` produces schema-valid data with plain Python, not a real model. Setting `models.ALLOW_MODEL_REQUESTS = False` blocks accidental requests to non-test models, but it doesn't supply a test model by itself.

sources.title: Unit testing
sources.claim: `Agent.override` replaces an agent's model, dependencies or toolsets inside application code; `TestModel` generates schema-valid data with procedural code and no ML; `models.ALLOW_MODEL_REQUESTS = False` blocks requests to non-test models.

questions.prompt: Your MCP server proxies a third-party API with one static OAuth client ID, and lets MCP clients register dynamically. Explain the confused deputy attack this allows, and what the server must do to prevent it.

model_answer.summary: Because the third-party authorization server remembers consent for the proxy's single client ID, an attacker's dynamically registered client can skip consent and receive an authorization code; the proxy must ask for its own per-client consent before forwarding and validate redirect URIs and `state` strictly.
key_points: After a user's first legitimate authorization, the third-party authorization server sets a consent cookie for the proxy's static client ID
An attacker registers a client with its own `redirect_uri` and sends the user a link; the cookie skips the consent screen and the MCP authorization code goes to the attacker
The proxy must keep a per-user registry of approved `client_id`s and show its own consent page, checked before it starts the third-party authorization
It must match `redirect_uri` exactly against the registered one and set a single-use, random `state` only after consent, checking it at the callback

questions.explanation: The third-party server sees every request as coming from the same client (the proxy), so its consent cookie can't tell a legitimate MCP client from an attacker's. The MCP security best practices therefore make the proxy responsible for consent per MCP client. Relying on the third-party consent screen alone is the tempting mistake.

sources.title: Security Best Practices
sources.claim: A proxy using a static client ID with a third-party authorization server, dynamic client registration and a consent cookie lets an attacker skip consent and receive an authorization code; proxies MUST implement per-client consent checked before third-party authorization, exact redirect_uri matching, and state set only after consent.

retired.reason: Written Questions are legacy (ADR-0008): replaced by a multiple-select Question on the same Concept.

questions.prompt: With the union `Annotated[Search | Reply | Handoff, Field(discriminator="kind")]`, the model returns `{"kind": "answer", "text": "hi"}`. No member has `kind` equal to `"answer"`. What error does Pydantic v2 raise?

choices.text: `union_tag_not_found`, because no member's tag could be found for it
No error: it validates as the closest member, which here is `Reply`
One error per member, since every model of the union fails in turn
`union_tag_invalid`, because the tag matches none of the members

questions.explanation: A discriminator value that matches no member's `Literal` raises `union_tag_invalid`, naming the tag and the expected ones. `union_tag_not_found` is for input where the discriminator field is missing altogether. A discriminated union never falls back to the closest match or tries every member.

sources.title: Unions
sources.claim: A missing discriminator value raises `union_tag_not_found`; a discriminator value that does not match any expected tag raises `union_tag_invalid`; only the member matching the discriminator is tried.

questions.prompt: Compare `TestModel` and `FunctionModel` for unit-testing a Pydantic AI agent. What does each do, and how do you get the test to use them without changing the agent?

model_answer.summary: `TestModel` generates schema-valid tool arguments and output with plain Python, while `FunctionModel` runs your own function to decide each response; swap either in with `Agent.override` and block real requests with `ALLOW_MODEL_REQUESTS = False`.
key_points: `TestModel` generates valid data for the agent's tools and output type from their schemas, using procedural code and no ML
`FunctionModel` calls a function you write, given the messages and agent info, so you control exactly which tools are called and what is returned
`agent.override(model=...)` swaps the model inside application code without changing the agent's definition
Set `models.ALLOW_MODEL_REQUESTS = False` so an accidental call to a real model fails, and use `capture_run_messages` to assert on the exchange

questions.explanation: `TestModel` is quick and checks that your tools and output schemas work, but its data is generic. When a test needs a specific path, such as one tool call followed by a particular answer, `FunctionModel` gives you that control. Both run offline, which is what makes the tests fast and free.

sources.title: Unit testing
sources.claim: TestModel generates valid structured data for tools and output types from their schemas with no ML; FunctionModel calls a user function given the messages and agent info; Agent.override replaces the model in application code; ALLOW_MODEL_REQUESTS = False blocks non-test model requests; capture_run_messages captures the exchange.

questions.prompt: In the confused deputy attack on an MCP proxy server, why does the third-party authorization server skip its consent screen for the attacker's request?

choices.text: Its consent cookie is for the proxy's static client ID, used by all
The attacker's newly registered client ID is approved by default
The proxy forwards the user's own access token, so no consent is due
PKCE lets the authorization server skip consent for known clients

questions.explanation: The proxy uses one static client ID with the third-party server for every MCP client. After the user's first approval, the third-party server's consent cookie covers that ID, so a request started by the attacker's client looks already approved. This is why the proxy itself must get consent per MCP client before forwarding.

sources.title: Security Best Practices
sources.claim: The third-party authorization server sets a consent cookie for the proxy's static client ID; when the user follows the attacker's link the cookie is present, so consent is skipped and the code is redirected to the attacker's registered redirect_uri.

questions.prompt: Your MCP server proxies a third-party API with one static OAuth client ID, and lets MCP clients register dynamically. Which statements about the confused deputy attack this allows, and its fix, are true? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Matching `redirect_uri` by prefix or wildcard is enough while the domain stays the same
A consent cookie for the proxy's static client ID lets a later request skip consent
An attacker registers a client with its own `redirect_uri` and gets the MCP auth code
The proxy checks its per-user list of approved `client_id`s before the third-party flow
Set the `state` cookie before showing the consent page, so the page can verify it

questions.explanation: After a user's first real authorization, the third-party server sets a consent cookie for the proxy's static client ID. An attacker then registers a client with its own `redirect_uri` and sends the user a link: the cookie skips the consent screen and the MCP authorization code goes to the attacker. The proxy MUST keep a per-user registry of approved `client_id`s and check it, with its own consent page, before starting the third-party flow. It MUST match `redirect_uri` exactly, never by pattern, and MUST NOT set the `state` cookie until after consent is approved.

sources.title: Security Best Practices
sources.claim: With a static client ID, dynamic client registration and a third-party consent cookie, an attacker's dynamically registered client with a malicious redirect_uri can skip consent and receive the MCP authorization code; MCP proxy servers MUST keep a registry of approved client_id values per user and check it before the third-party flow, validate redirect_uri by exact string matching (not patterns or wildcards), and set the state cookie only after consent is approved.

questions.prompt: You are unit-testing a Pydantic AI agent without calling a real LLM. Which statements about `TestModel`, `FunctionModel` and the related helpers are true? Select all that apply.

choices.text: `TestModel` makes schema-valid tool arguments and output with plain code, no ML
`TestModel` sends prompts to a small hosted model, so the tests need network access
`FunctionModel` calls a function you write, so you decide which tools get called
`agent.override(model=...)` swaps the model without changing the agent definition
`ALLOW_MODEL_REQUESTS = False` makes real model calls return canned empty replies

questions.explanation: `TestModel` generates valid data for tools and output types from their schemas with procedural Python, no ML and no network. `FunctionModel` replaces the model with a function you write, given the messages and agent info, so you control the tool calls and replies. `agent.override(model=...)` swaps the model inside application code without editing the agent. Setting `models.ALLOW_MODEL_REQUESTS = False` is a safety net that stops accidental real requests to an LLM; it doesn't fake replies.

sources.title: Unit testing
sources.claim: TestModel generates valid structured data for tools and output types from their schemas with plain procedural Python, no ML; FunctionModel calls a user-defined function with the messages and agent info; Agent.override replaces an agent's model inside application code; `models.ALLOW_MODEL_REQUESTS = False` prevents accidental real requests to an LLM during tests.
